content: 1. Administer intravenous fluids rapidly if the patient is in shock, has a systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg, a pulse rate exceeding 110 beats per minute, or is experiencing heavy vaginal bleeding. Infuse 1 liter of fluid within 15–20 minutes as quickly as possible. If necessary, repeat the infusion. Monitor the patient every 15 minutes for blood pressure, pulse, shortness of breath, or signs of fluid overload. Once the pulse slows to below 100 beats per minute and systolic blood pressure rises to 100 mmHg or higher, reduce the infusion rate to 3 ml/min (1 liter over 6–8 hours). If breathing difficulty or puffiness develops, reduce the rate further to 5 ml/min. Record the time and amount of fluids administered and monitor urine output. 2. For severe abdominal pain, obstructed labor, ectopic pregnancy, dangerous fever, or dehydration, administer fluids at a moderate rate, infusing 1 liter over 2–3 hours. 3. For severe anemia, severe pre-eclampsia, or eclampsia, administer fluids at a slow rate, infusing 1 liter over 6–8 hours. 4. If intravenous access is not possible, provide oral rehydration solution (ORS) if the patient can drink, or administer it via a nasogastric tube. Use 300–500 ml of ORS over 1 hour. Do not give ORS to unconscious patients or those experiencing convulsions. 5. In cases of heavy postpartum bleeding, massage the uterus to encourage contraction and expel clots. Place a cupped palm on the uterine fundus, assess the state of contraction, and massage in a circular motion until the uterus is firm. Once contracted, apply downward pressure to expel clots. Collect and measure blood loss, recording the amount. 6. If heavy postpartum bleeding persists despite uterine massage, oxytocin/ergometrine treatment, and removal of the placenta, apply bimanual uterine compression. Insert a sterile gloved hand into the vagina, place the other hand on the abdomen behind the uterus, and firmly compress the uterus between the two hands until bleeding stops. If bleeding continues, apply aortic compression by pressing above the umbilicus to stop blood flow. Ensure the femoral pulse is not palpable. If necessary, train an assistant to maintain pressure until the patient can be transported to a hospital. 7. Administer oxytocin for heavy postpartum bleeding. The initial dose is 10 IU intramuscularly or intravenously. If bleeding persists, repeat 10 IU after 20 minutes. For intravenous infusion, administer 20 IU in 1 liter of fluid at 60 drops/min or 10 IU in 1 liter at 30 drops/min. Do not exceed 3 liters of IV fluids containing oxytocin. 8. If oxytocin is unavailable or ineffective, administer misoprostol (800 µg) sublingually. Alternatively, administer ergometrine for heavy bleeding in early pregnancy or postpartum, but avoid it in cases of eclampsia, pre-eclampsia, hypertension, or retained placenta. 9. If the placenta is not delivered within 1 hour after childbirth or if heavy bleeding continues despite controlled cord traction, perform manual removal of the placenta. Explain the procedure to the patient and obtain consent. Insert an IV line and administer fluids rapidly if bleeding is present. Assist the patient into a supine position, administer diazepam (10 mg IM/IV), and ensure the bladder is empty. Using sterile gloves, insert the right hand into the uterus to detach the placenta gradually, ensuring all fragments are removed. If the placenta does not separate easily, suspect placenta accreta and refer the patient urgently to a hospital. 10. After manual removal of the placenta, administer 10 IU of oxytocin IM/IV and massage the uterine fundus to encourage contraction. Administer antibiotics such as ampicillin (2 g IV/IM) and gentamicin (80 mg IM) if there are signs of infection or prolonged rupture of membranes. If bleeding stops, continue fluids slowly for at least 1 hour. 11. For eclampsia or severe pre-eclampsia, administer magnesium sulfate as a loading dose: 4 g IV slowly over 20 minutes and 10 g IM (5 g in each buttock with 1 ml of 2% lignocaine). If IV access is unavailable, give 10 g IM only. Monitor for signs of magnesium toxicity, such as absent knee reflexes, urine output below 100 ml/4 hours, or respiratory rate below 16 breaths/min. If toxicity occurs, stop magnesium sulfate and administer calcium gluconate (1 g IV over 10 minutes). 12. If convulsions recur, administer an additional 2 g of magnesium sulfate IV over 20 minutes. If convulsions persist, administer diazepam (10 mg IV slowly over 2 minutes). For maintenance, give 5 g of magnesium sulfate IM every 4 hours in alternate buttocks for up to 24 hours after delivery or the last convulsion. 13. For hypertension with diastolic blood pressure >110 mmHg, administer hydralazine 5 mg IV slowly over 3–4 minutes. If IV access is unavailable, give IM. Repeat every 30 minutes until diastolic BP is around 90 mmHg. 14. For infections, administer appropriate IV/IM antibiotics such as ampicillin (2 g IV/IM initially, then 1 g every 6 hours), gentamicin (80 mg IM every 8 hours), and metronidazole (500 mg IV every 8 hours). If referral is delayed, continue antibiotics for 48 hours after the patient is fever-free, then switch to oral amoxicillin (500 mg three times daily) to complete 7 days of treatment. 15. For malaria, confirm diagnosis with parasitological testing. Administer artesunate or quinine IM as per national guidelines. Always provide glucose with quinine. If referral is delayed, continue treatment and refer after delivery if necessary. 16. For severe febrile illness treated with quinine, administer IV glucose (e.g., 50% glucose solution, 25–50 ml; 25% glucose solution, 50–100 ml; or 10% glucose solution, 125–250 ml) to prevent hypoglycemia. Ensure the IV drip is functioning properly.
